extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (Patent Examining Corps); also patent practitioners and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on evaluating subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), specifically whether an additional element or combination of elements is 'well‑understood, routine, conventional' for step 2B. Includes required factual support and permissible types of evidence when formulating or maintaining an eligibility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether an additional element is well‑understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether something is well‑understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan at the time of the patent is a factual determination. The additional elements must be 'widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field,' comparable to activities or elements so well‑known that they need not be described in detail in a patent application to satisfy 35 U.S.C. §112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inquiry is distinct from novelty or obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §§102/103; mere disclosure in prior art does not by itself establish conventionality. Examiners should follow MPEP §2106.05(d)(I) and support any conclusion with factual evidence as described in the memorandum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating rejections — citation to specification or applicant statements
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may support a step 2B rejection by citing an express statement in the specification or a statement made by an applicant during prosecution that demonstrates the well‑understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification demonstrates conventionality when it describes the additional elements as well‑understood, routine, or conventional (or equivalent terms), as a commercially available product, or in a manner indicating the elements are sufficiently well‑known that particulars need not be described to satisfy 35 U.S.C. §112(a). A finding of conventionality cannot be based only on the specification's silence about an element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating rejections — citation to court decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may support a step 2B rejection by citing one or more court decisions (e.g., decisions discussed in MPEP §2106.05(d)(II)) that note the well‑understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent where the court expressly characterizes the element(s) as well‑understood, routine, or conventional in the relevant field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating rejections — citation to publications demonstrating conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may support a step 2B rejection by citing a publication (book, manual, review article, or other source) that demonstrates the additional element(s) are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all items that qualify as a 'printed publication' under 35 U.S.C. §102 will suffice. The nature of the publication and how it describes the additional elements must demonstrate they are widely prevalent or in common use (comparable to items so well‑known they need not be described in a patent to satisfy §112(a)). A single patent or published application typically will not be sufficient unless it demonstrates widespread prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating rejections — official notice by examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may state that he or she is taking official notice of the well‑understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This option should be used only when the examiner is certain, based upon personal knowledge, that the additional element(s) are widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field (comparable to activities that need not be described in detail to satisfy §112(a)). Procedures for taking official notice and responding to applicant challenges are in MPEP §2144.03. If official notice is taken and applicant challenges it, the examiner must then provide one of the evidentiary items (spec/applicant statement, court decision, publication) or an affidavit/declaration as discussed below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant's response to a conventionality assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant challenges the examiner's position that additional element(s) are well‑understood, routine, conventional, the examiner should reevaluate whether the elements are in fact well‑understood, routine, conventional to those in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner relied on official notice and the applicant specifically challenges it, the examiner must provide one of the evidentiary items described above (spec/applicant statement, court decision, publication) or an affidavit/declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.104(d)(2) setting forth specific factual statements and explanation to support the position. The examiner's factual conclusion must be supported as discussed in the memorandum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between conventionality inquiry and §§102/103 patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing that additional elements are obvious under 35 U.S.C. §103, or lack novelty under 35 U.S.C. §102, is not by itself sufficient to establish that the additional elements are well‑understood, routine, conventional activities or elements in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere fact that something appears in prior art does not mean it was well‑understood, routine, and conventional. Examiners must go beyond prior art disclosure and show prevalence/common use as required for the conventionality finding under step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to 35 U.S.C. §112(a) enablement/written description analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of whether an element (or combination of elements) is widely prevalent or in common use is the same as the analysis under 35 U.S.C. §112(a) as to whether an element is so well‑known that it need not be described in detail in the patent specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Genetic Techs., Lindemann, In re Myers) supports treating elements that need not be described because they are well known in the art as evidence of conventionality; however, silence in the specification alone is insufficient to support conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that recite limitations directed to purported improvements may raise factual issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that include limitations reflecting purported improvements described in the specification (e.g., 'storing ... without substantial redundancy' resulting in improved system efficiency) can raise a genuine issue of material fact as to whether those limitations are more than well‑understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims include limitations tied to concrete improvements described in the specification, examiners should consider whether the claim limitations are themselves unconventional in light of the factual-record support; such claims may preclude summary rejection on eligibility until fact‑finding is complete (as illustrated by Berkheimer's reversal of summary judgment for claims reciting such improvements).
